summary: Describes a mechanism for a restarting IS-IS router to tell its neighbors, so they can rebuild adjacencies without cycling through the down state while still starting database synchronization. It also lets a router warn neighbors that it is about to restart while keeping its forwarding state.

plainLanguage.summary: When a router reboots, it tells neighbors that it will be right back, so they do not assume it vanished and reroute everything.

questions: what is the is-is restart tlv
what do the rr ra sa pr pa flags mean in is-is
subtitle: How an IS-IS router tells its neighbors it is restarting, so they keep the adjacency instead of tearing it down and rerouting traffic.

tldr.problem: When an IS-IS router restarts, its neighbors normally cycle their adjacency with it through the DOWN state and regenerate their LSPs, which temporarily disrupts routes through the restarting router. The restarted router can also compute routes before its database is synchronized.
tldr.mechanism: A new Restart TLV (type 211) in IS-IS Hello PDUs carries flags that announce a restart, acknowledge it, suppress an adjacency advertisement, or announce a planned restart. Three timers (T1, T2, T3) drive the exchange and the database synchronization.
tldr.outcome: Neighbors keep the adjacency up and resend their database summaries, the restarting router waits until its LSP database is synchronized, and traffic keeps flowing. RFC 8706 obsoletes RFC 5306 and adds the planned-restart signal.

today: RFC 8706 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2020. It obsoletes RFC 5306, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it according to the unit metadata.

sections.title: The Restart Problem in IS-IS
sections.content:
IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System) is a link state routing protocol that routes inside one domain. Normally, a restart causes temporary routing disruption from two sources: the restarted router computes its own routes before its database is synchronized with its neighbors, and the neighbors see the restart, cycle their adjacency through the DOWN state and regenerate their LSPs.

When an adjacency is reinitialized, a router does three things: it regenerates its own LSPs (which triggers SPF runs in the area), it sets SRMflags on its LSP database for that adjacency, and on a point-to-point link it sends a complete set of CSNPs. The RFC says the first is highly undesirable for a restarting router, but the second is essential to get the LSP database synchronized.

RFC 8706 describes a way for a restarting router to signal its neighbors so they can reestablish the adjacency without cycling through DOWN while still starting database synchronization. It also describes how the restarting router learns that synchronization is done, and how to optimize synchronization when a router starts. It assumes the three-way handshake of RFC 5303 is used on point-to-point circuits.
sections.plainLanguage: If a teacher steps out of class for a minute and nobody knows why, the class might send for a substitute. A note on the door saying "back in a minute" avoids that fuss.

sections.title: Restarting, Starting and the Three Timers
sections.content:
The RFC separates two cases. A restarting router has kept its forwarding state while its control function restarted, which is only possible if the two functions can be maintained independently. A starting router has either started for the first time or resumed without maintained forwarding state. The term "(re)start" covers both.

Three timers support the mechanism. T1 is kept per interface and sets when an unacknowledged (re)start attempt is repeated; a typical value is 3 seconds. T2 is kept for each LSP database and is the longest the system waits for synchronization; a typical value is 60 seconds. T3 is a single timer for the whole system, used only by a restarting router. It starts at 65535 seconds and is lowered to the smallest remaining time reported by acknowledging neighbors. If it expires, the router sets the overload bit in its own LSP. These timers do not apply to a router preparing a planned restart.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three egg timers. One says "ask again if nobody answered," one says "stop waiting to catch up after this long," and one says "our neighbors will give up on us soon."

sections.title: The Restart TLV
sections.content:
The mechanism rests on one new TLV, the Restart TLV, which is carried only in IS-IS Hello PDUs (IIHs). Its type is 211. If a router supports any functionality in this document, it MUST include the TLV in every IIH it sends; a missing TLV tells the receiver that the sender supports none of it.

The value holds a one-octet flags field, a two-octet Remaining Time (remaining holding time in seconds, required when RA, PR or PA is set), and a Restarting Neighbor System ID of ID Length octets (required when RA or PA is set). The Remaining Time and Neighbor ID SHOULD be omitted otherwise and MUST be ignored if received.

The five flags are RR (restart request), RA (restart acknowledgement), SA (suppress adjacency advertisement), PR (restart is planned) and PA (planned restart acknowledgement). RR and SA may both be set together when a router starts; all other combinations of flags are invalid, MUST NOT be sent, and are ignored when received.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a little sticker on each "hello" message with five checkboxes: asking for help, saying thanks, "do not tell others about me yet," "I will leave soon," and "okay, I know."

sections.title: Signaling a Restart, a Start or a Planned Restart
sections.content:
A restarting router sends IIHs with RR set. A neighbor that has an adjacency in the UP state with that router leaves the adjacency state unchanged, marks it as in "Restart mode", refreshes the holding time the first time only, immediately replies with an IIH carrying RA and the Remaining Time, and sends a complete set of CSNPs and sets SRMflags. On a LAN the CSNPs come from the neighbor with the highest priority among those not in Restart mode. A router that does not support the feature ignores the TLV and reinitializes the adjacency as usual.

A starting router has no maintained forwarding state, so copies of its old LSPs elsewhere may look newer than its fresh ones and cause temporary blackholes. It therefore sends IIHs with SA set, and neighbors MUST suppress the advertisement of that adjacency in their LSPs, and not use it in their own SPF, until an IIH with SA clear arrives.

A router that plans a restart sends PR with a Remaining Time greater than the expected control-plane restart time. Neighbors mark the adjacency as being in Planned Restart State, answer with PA, and SHOULD keep the adjacency until they see RR, an IIH with PR and RR both clear, or the holding time expires. While it is in that state, a neighbor MAY still bring the adjacency down if other topology changes happen, because the restarting router cannot update its forwarding plane in the meantime. Signaling a planned restart without maintained forwarding-plane state MUST NOT be done.
sections.plainLanguage: A rebooting router waves a flag that says "I am back, please send me everything I missed." A router that knows it will leave soon says so ahead of time, and its friends promise to wait a while.

sections.title: Database Synchronization and Holding Back LSPs
sections.content:
After a (re)start the router expects a complete set of CSNPs on each interface; the RR bit is retransmitted until they arrive. It records the LSP IDs listed in the first complete set (ignoring LSPs with remaining lifetime of zero) and removes each entry as the matching LSP arrives. When the list is empty and T1 has been canceled on all interfaces at that level, T2 is canceled and the database is deemed synchronized.

A restarting router does not transmit its own LSPs and does not update its forwarding tables while T3 runs, so the LSPs it later floods can match the old ones and avoid churn elsewhere. It does not purge its own LSPs that it receives in the meantime. When T2 for a level expires or is canceled, SPF runs for that level without updating forwarding tables, and its own LSPs are generated and flooded after inter-level information is resolved. When all T2 timers are done, T3 is canceled and the forwarding tables are updated. If T3 expires first, the router floods its LSPs with the overload bit set so others do not route through it, and sends normal IIHs so neighbors keep their adjacencies.

A starting router sends its zeroth LSP with the overload bit set as soon as each adjacency is up and before CSNP exchange, and clears it only after all T2 timers are canceled. Its IIHs carry SA until then, and it MUST then send IIHs with SA clear.
sections.plainLanguage: The returning router first listens quietly to catch up on what changed. Only when it is sure it has the full story does it start talking and moving traffic again.

sections.title: Security and Manageability
sections.content:
The RFC says any new security issues depend on an attacker being able to inject a false but apparently valid IIH, which is no easier or harder than before. A false IIH with RR only makes neighbors keep an adjacency and possibly resend CSNPs, which is wasteful but does not break correct operation. A false RA could make a (re)starting router wrongly believe a neighbor supports the feature and delay completion until T1 times out. A false SA could suppress an advertised neighbor and so cause loss of reachability or extra flooding and SPF runs.

A false PR could make a neighbor change a holding time inappropriately or avoid bringing down an adjacency after topology changes, and a false PA could lead a router to restart when the neighbor will not wait. The RFC recommends reducing spoofing with IS-IS authentication, especially cryptographic authentication from RFC 5304 and RFC 5310. Under manageability, it states that these extensions, developed and deployed over many years, add no new management impact.
sections.plainLanguage: A prankster could send a fake "I am restarting" note and confuse the neighbors. Signing the messages so they cannot be faked is the fix the RFC recommends.

sections.title: What Changed from RFC 5306
sections.content:
RFC 8706 extends RFC 5306 by adding support for signaling that a planned restart is about to happen. The motivation is that, because the forwarding plane of the restarting router is kept based on the pre-restart state of the network, other topology changes could lose traffic if paths through it keep being used during the restart.

Two new flags carry this: PR (restart is planned) and PA (planned restart acknowledgement). The appendix states that no changes were made to the exchange between the restarting router and its neighbors after the restart. The RFC also notes that early drafts left out the Restarting Neighbor System ID, and leaves it to implementations whether to keep accepting an RA without it on a LAN.
sections.plainLanguage: The old rule only covered "I am back." The update adds "I am about to leave for a bit," so friends can plan ahead.

items.label: Restart Request
items.desc: A (re)starting router asks neighbors to keep the adjacency, send CSNPs and set SRMflags.

items.label: Suppress adjacency advertisement
items.desc: A starting router asks neighbors not to advertise the adjacency yet.

items.label: Restart is planned
items.desc: A router warns neighbors that it is about to restart.
